results.title: Blackwell GPU rental prices hit $4.08 an hour. Sixty days earlier, they were 48% cheaper. | Jonathan Mather
highlights: Blackwell GPU rental prices hit $4.08 an hour. Sixty days earlier, they were 48% cheaper. Not over a year. Over two months. AWS's flagship 8x H200 instance went from $34.61 an hour to $39.80 in the same stretch. Lead times for data-center GPUs now run 36 to 52 weeks. Order today, plan for delivery next year, if it clears at all. A training run budgeted at $40,000 on reserved capacity is now $80,000 to $120,000 on-demand, if the capacity is reachable at any price. Here's why it's scarce, and it doesn't resolve itself. Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon placed multi-billion-dollar forward orders for Blackwell chips that already consumed most of Nvidia's available allocation through 2027. That's not four companies competing for GPUs alongside you. That's four companies who bought the shelf before you got to the store. This isn't a future risk. The compute shortage is already causing outages at Anthropic and has forced OpenAI to cancel products. If the two best-capitalized AI companies on the planet are getting squeezed this hard, paying a premium to route around it isn't a real option for anyone smaller. Memory prices are surging at the same time. TSMC capacity is effectively sold out. Power infrastructure is now a hard bottleneck in its own right. Every layer of the stack tightened at once. Bank of America's own projection: demand outstrips supply through 2029. Not a temporary crunch. A multi-year structural gap. If your AI roadmap assumes 2025 pricing and 2025 availability, it's already obsolete. The real question isn't "can we afford the GPU-hours." It's whether your architecture depends on owning or reserving compute at all, because the companies with the deepest pockets just found out the answer is no, not reliably. Has the compute shortage already hit your roadmap, or are you still budgeting off last quarter's numbers?

박재현 기자

[사진=픽사베이]

[디지털데일리 박재현기자] 유휴 GPU(그래픽처리장치) 재임대 시장이 확대되고 있다. AI 서비스 수익화가 늦어지면서 인프라 고정비 부담을 안은 기업이 늘어난 영향이다. 몬드리안에이아이의 '런유어 AI', 베슬에이아이(VESSL AI)의 '베슬 클라우드'가 대표적이다.

두 서비스는 자체 GPU를 파는 방식이 아니다. 기업이나 기관에서 보유했지만 사용하지 않는 유휴 GPU를 수요자에게 판매할 수 있도록 중개하는 방식이다. 런유어 AI는 GPU 소유자와 수요자를 연결하는 중개형 플랫폼이다. 온디맨드와 장기계약을 함께 제공하며, 역경매 방식의 '리서브 클라우드'로 중소 데이터센터의 유휴 자원을 수익화한다. 베슬에이아이는 자체 데이터센터 없이 6개국 GPU를 연결하는 구조를 택했다. 현재 5000장 규모를 운용 중이며 연내 1만장까지 확대한다는 계획이다.

가격은 하이퍼스케일러보다 낮다. 런유어 AI는 H100 SXM 80GB를 시간당 3615원(3615C), B200을 9351원으로 책정했다. 베슬에이아이는 H100 온디맨드 요금이 시간당 2.98달러(약 4330원)로 하이퍼스케일러 절반 수준이라고 밝혔다.

대학 연구실과 스타트업이 주요 고객이다. 국내 한 대학 연구실 관계자는 "상용 퍼블릭 클라우드는 예산 한계가 명확했다"며 "재임대 플랫폼으로 같은 비용에 훨씬 큰 GPU 자원을 장기 확보했다"고 말했다.

수요 성격도 달라지는 추세다. 단기·소규모 대여보다 장기·대규모 대여 비중이 커지고 있다. 비용 절감보다 연구 확대를 위한 수요가 늘어난 결과다. 유휴 자원을 등록하는 공급 기업도 서서히 증가하고 있다.

...

시장 확대와 별개로 계약 리스크는 남아 있다. CSP 이용약관은 서비스 재판매와 전대를 금지한다. 네이버클라우드는 회사 동의 없이 제3자에게 서비스를 재판매·재임대할 수 없다고 규정했다. KT클라우드와 AWS도 동일한 취지의 조항을 두고 있다.

정식 플랫폼은 이 조항에 저촉되지 않는다는 입장이다. 홍대의 몬드리안에이아이 대표는 "자사는 CSP 임차 장비를 재임대하지 않는다"며 "CSP가 직접 공급하거나 기업이 자체 보유한 GPU를 재임대하는 형태"라고 말했다.

results.title: The GPU Market Has Two Prices | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
A hyperscaler quotes $10.60 an hour for an H200. A wholesale buyer gets the same chip for $3.79 to $4.54. Neither number is fake. Both are real prices for the same GPU, quoted to two different buyers in two different markets.

Most enterprise buyers only ever see one of those markets.

Key takeaways

- H100 retail held steady at $25,000 to $40,000 from mid-2024 into early 2026, while the secondary market swung from $50,000 during 2024's scarcity peak down to $21,000-$34,000 refurbished as of Q2 2026
- Hyperscaler H200 on-demand runs around $10.60/hr versus $3.79 to $4.54/hr wholesale for the same silicon
- A100 cloud rental rates range $1.29 to $3.43/hr depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread for the same chip
- The retail price is quoted to whoever asks casually. The clearing price moves with real-time supply and demand among buyers actually transacting
- Q2 2026 secondary supply is loosening further as B200 deployments accelerate, with continued softening expected on H100 and A100 inventory specifically

...

The same split shows up in rental rates, not just purchase price. Hyperscaler on-demand carries a premium built for buyers who need the full managed stack, global region coverage, compliance certification, native tooling. Specialized providers price the same H200 silicon closer to what the hardware costs to run, without the bundle. Both numbers are legitimate. They're pricing different things wrapped around the same chip.

...

The gap doesn't stay constant either. Q2 2026 secondary supply is loosening further as B200 deployments accelerate and legacy contract inventory flows back into circulation. Continued softening expected on H100 and A100 inventory specifically, the exact segment where the retail-versus-real gap has been widest.

...

For H200, hyperscaler on-demand runs around $10.60 an hour versus $3.79 to $4.54 an hour wholesale for the same silicon. For A100 rentals, rates range $1.29 to $3.43 an hour depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread. These gaps vary by chip generation and current market conditions.

Spot (also called preemptible or interruptible) is the same GPU sold for less on the condition that the provider can take it back when it needs the capacity, usually with a short warning ( spot). Against a provider's own on-demand rate, the discount is the figure providers advertise, and the live figures say how large it is. On the H100 SXM right now, AWS's spot rate is -88% against its on-demand rate, Google Cloud's -80%, CoreWeave's -60% and Verda's -50%. The spot vs on-demand page lists every provider's spot discount, card by card.

But the comparison that matters to a buyer is spot against the whole market's on-demand floor, not against the same provider's on-demand rate, and there spot is not automatically the cheaper line. A marketplace host renting a card on demand can undercut a big cloud's spot capacity, because the host's price is set by competition among hosts rather than as a discount on a cloud's list price. The table puts the cheapest spot rate anywhere beside the cheapest on-demand rate anywhere. Spot vs floor is the spot rate against the floor: a negative figure means spot is cheaper, a positive one means the on-demand floor already beats every spot rate.

The providers in the tables above are not interchangeable, and the kind of seller is the first thing to know about any rate in the first table ( hyperscaler, neocloud, marketplace). The reason is structural rather than a matter of generosity. A marketplace (Vast.ai, Clore.ai, SaladCloud, RunPod's Community Cloud) rents machines that independent hosts already own, and hosts compete listing by listing, so prices move with supply and the reliability is the host's. A GPU cloud (Lambda, Nebius, CoreWeave, Hyperstack, Verda and many others, sometimes called neoclouds) owns or leases data-center fleets and sells them at published rates, with data-center networking, support and, at some, an uptime commitment. A serverless platform (Modal, DeepInfra, Koyeb and others) bills only while your code runs and scales to zero between requests, so its hourly rate (Modal's H100 is $3.95, 2.1x the floor) is paid only for the seconds you use ( serverless GPU). A hyperscaler (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle) sells the GPU as one part of a whole platform, priced for the customers who need the rest of it.

Today's cheapest seller is not always tomorrow's. FastGPU records which provider held each card's cheapest price every morning, and how often each provider holds it, card by card, and how often it changes hands is counted on which GPU cloud is cheapest, day by day.

On-demand is the right default for anything that runs less than most of the day. For a steady load that runs around the clock for months, reserved capacity trades a commitment for a lower hourly rate ( reserved capacity), and the arithmetic of whether it pays is one division. A reservation is owed every hour whether the GPU works or not, so it beats on-demand only if the GPU would otherwise be busy for more than the reserved rate divided by the on-demand rate of all hours. Hyperstack's reserved H100 SXM rate is $2.72 against its own on-demand rate of $3.20 ( -15%), so the break-even share is 0.85 ($2.72 / $3.20): reserving pays only if the GPU would be busy for more than that share of all hours, and never if the share is 1 or more.

That comparison is against the same provider's on-demand rate, and the open market can change it. The H100 SXM floor of $1.84 is below that reserved rate with no commitment at all, and the A100 80GB floor of $0.84 is below Hyperstack's reserved A100 80GB rate of $0.95. A reservation buys certainty that the GPUs are yours, which the floor does not promise, so the fair question is what that certainty is worth to your job, not whether the reserved rate is "cheap". The reserve vs rent calculator does the break-even for any card and term with the posted reserved rates in the feed.

results.title: India's Blackwell GPU cloud in 2026: rent domestic, tap IndiaAI, or go hyperscaler? - DEV Community
highlights:
Summary. In July 2026 Yotta Data Services raised USD 150 million at a valuation near ₹37,000 crore and said it will scale its AI cloud to about 85,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs by the end of its financial year, up from the 8,192 H100 GPUs it already runs at Navi Mumbai. At the same time the IndiaAI Mission has put roughly 38,000 GPUs on tap at about ₹65 per hour, roughly 72 US cents, through 14 empanelled providers. That changes the build-versus-rent maths for Indian teams. A single Blackwell B200 on a global hyperscaler runs about USD 6 per GPU-hour on-demand as of March 2026, and a GB200 rack slice runs USD 12 to 18. Domestic H100 capacity at E2E Networks lists at ₹249 per hour. This guide is a decision framework: when domestic sovereign cloud, the subsidised IndiaAI pool, or a global hyperscaler is the right call, weighed on price, data residency, latency and availability rather than on any single number.

...

| Decision vector | Domestic sovereign cloud (Yotta, E2E) | IndiaAI Mission pool | Global hyperscaler (AWS, Azure, GCP) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Headline price signal | ₹249/hr H100 at E2E; Blackwell by contract | About ₹65 per GPU-hour, subsidised | About USD 6/hr B200; USD 12 to 18 GB200 |
| Data residency | In India, DPDP-aligned by design | In India, government facility | Region-dependent; India regions exist |
| Availability today | H100 now; B200 and B300 landing through FY27 | Allocation-based, eligibility-gated | Broad, but Blackwell still waitlisted |
| Managed services depth | Growing; storage and platform partners | Bare compute plus portal tooling | Deepest: databases, networking, MLOps |
| Best fit | Regulated data, steady training, BFSI and government | Startups, research, MSMEs, price-first | Global products, spiky inference, rich tooling |

...

## Cost: what a GPU-hour actually costs in 2026

Price is where the domestic story is strongest, but the comparison has to be honest about GPU generation. Much of India's cheap domestic capacity today is H100 and H200 class; Blackwell B200 and B300 pricing at Yotta and E2E is largely enterprise-contract and not published, while the hyperscaler figures below are for Blackwell parts that are newer than the domestic H100 they undercut.

| Option | GPU | Indicative price | Source basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E2E Networks (India) | H100 on-demand | ₹249 per hour | Provider list price, 2026 |
| E2E Networks (India) | H100 spot | ₹70 per hour | Provider list price, 2026 |
| IndiaAI Mission | Subsidised pool | About ₹65 per GPU-hour | IndiaAI Compute Portal, 2026 |
| IndiaAI empanelled | Unsubsidised | ₹115 to ₹150 per GPU-hour | Empanelment bids, 2026 |
| Global hyperscaler | B200 on-demand | About USD 6 per GPU-hour | Market rate, March 2026 |
| Global hyperscaler | GB200 slice | USD 12 to 18 per GPU-hour | Early-adopter rate, 2026 |

Two numbers frame the gap. The IndiaAI Mission rate of about ₹65 per hour is under one US dollar, and government analysis puts empanelled rates 40 to 60 percent below global cloud on-demand pricing. On the other side, the median on-demand B200 price across providers rose about 11 percent between July 2025 and 2026, from USD 5.50 to about USD 6.12 per GPU-hour, because Blackwell demand still outruns supply. For a price-sensitive training run on H100-class silicon, domestic is not a little cheaper; it is a different order of cost. For teams that need the newest Blackwell parts at scale today, the hyperscalers still have the deepest pools, which is why our India GPU cloud rental pricing breakdown treats availability as a first-class variable alongside the rate.
